It feels like no one has ever actually tried to reset a password. Not for real. What I mean is that if a system forces me to change my password every sixty days, and it is not just one character but a jumbled mess of symbols, and if I type it wrong once, I am locked out. And if I really want to change it, I am forced to remember the old password, and if I do not, I need to reset it. And that is if I am lucky. That is the process. And it is insane.

Of course, security people will say, "No, it is to protect you." It is not to protect you. It is to protect themselves. And it is a good argument. And the reason for this is because there are credential stuffing attacks, which is where a site gets breached, and they have a list of passwords, and they just try every one of them. If it works, then it works. So it is a massive attack. And if you do not have a lockout, it is very easy to do. And so it is true that people should change their passwords. But the problem is that if you force a change, the user will do a small change. So if the password is something like "Password123" for example, it will be "Password124". So the attacker will guess it. And people also reuse passwords. They will put the same password on different sites. And when one site gets breached, then all the sites get breached. So it is a vicious cycle. And so the argument is that forced resets do not actually work. It is a security theater. And the standard, the NIST standard, says do not force it. It says do not force the complexity. They say, just use a long passphrase. Check it against the list of breached passwords. So if it is in a breach, change it. But do not force it. But if it is a high-risk environment, if it is a financial system or an admin console, then it makes sense to be stricter. But it makes sense to have a risk-based policy. So not everyone needs the same policy. And that is the problem.

And on the usability side, it is really bad. It is really bad. So what we see is a lot of password resets. So we are very busy with password resets. And it is not good. It is not good. And if you make it hard, then people will write it down, or they will reuse it, or they will not use the system. And it is a massive thing. And self-service password reset is the standard now. But it is risky. Because if they can get into your email, they can reset your password and get into your account. And they can get into your email. So it is risky. And they also used to ask questions. So, what is your mother's maiden name? And you know what? People put it on Facebook. So it is not secure. So you have to do it right. You have to verify identity, but you have to do it well. You have to do multi-factor. So, on reset, you have to verify. And you should use the same method that you are using to log in. So, if you have MFA for login, you have to use it for reset. And it is better to use a hardware token, or a mobile device, or something like that. So you have to do it properly. But if you can do that, you can make it easier. And it is very easy. And if you use MFA, it is easy. And it is much more secure.

So the idea is risk-based authentication. So, on reset, I am going to look at the signals. So, where are you coming from? What device? What time? Are you doing something unusual? If you are doing something unusual, it is risky, so you have to verify. If you are doing something normal, you can verify it lightly. So, if you are coming from your office IP on your computer, you can probably just get an email and reset it. But if you are coming from some random country, and it is a random device, you have to do something. So, that is the whole idea. And it is not the same. So, an admin that is resetting the password for the payroll system, they have to do more verification. If it is a low-risk user, that is just an employee that is resetting the password for the wiki, they do not have to do so much. So, it is risk-based. And that is the way to go.

And how do you implement that? So, you have to have a system. And it is not easy. So, you have to have a policy. And you have to do things. So, first of all, you have to stop the expiration. So, stop the forced reset. And then you have to have the user create a strong password. And then you have to check it against the breached passwords. And you have to do it every time. And you have to do rate limiting. So, they cannot make a million requests. And you have to do lockout. And you have to do exponential backoff. So, they try again, they try again, and it takes longer. And so, that is for brute force. And then you have to have a nice, clear process. And you have to tell them what is happening. And you should not do security questions. And you should do multi-factor. And you should send alerts. So, if you reset your password, you should get an email. And then, if you did not reset it, you can say, "What is going on?" And then you can check the logs. And you should have logs of all of this. And you should train people. You should tell them what to do. And they have to understand it. And they have to trust it. And if they trust it, they are going to do it. And you should review it. So, you should look at your policy and say, is this still good? Is this still good? Because things change. And if it is not, change it.

So, the argument is that it is too complex, it is too expensive. And it is true. It is more expensive. And it is more complex. And it is not easy. And legacy systems are not going to do it. So, if you are a small organization, it is not going to be easy. But the cost of a bad policy is high. And it is high. So, you can do it in phases. You can do it. So, first, take out the expiration. Add the breached password check. Then add multi-factor. Then add the risk. And over time, you can do it. And it is not perfect, but it is better. And that is the goal.

And so, in conclusion, it should not be a test of your endurance. It should be a gate. It should be a gate that protects you, but not too much. And it should be risk-based. And it should be multi-factor. And it should be clear. And it should be easy. And if it is easy, they are going to do it. And if it is easy and they trust it, they are going to do it. And that is the whole point. So, make it work.

text:
The robot vacuum was not something Harold wanted. It came in a box, the size of a small cake, and his daughter Claire unpacked it on the kitchen table. She was treating it like a birthday. Inside, the disc was black and very smooth. The texture was something like a river stone. There was only one button on it. Claire said that it would change his life. Harold did not believe that. The vacuum made a sound, like a chirp, four notes going up. Then it started to turn. It moved in slow circles, like a dog deciding where to lay down.

He watched it from the doorway. It moved with a very patient purpose. The way it moved seemed sad, maybe. It bumped against the baseboard and then went back. Then it tried again. The red eye was spinning under there. It learned the geography of the house in an afternoon, which was something Harold was not going to do. It was mapping the house. He'd been living there forty-one years. He knew the geography. The vacuum knew the walls and thresholds, the places where the floor went down around the radiator. The hall closet door was swollen. It wouldn't close all the way. It knew that before he did. The vacuum learned the house.

At night, it would hum in its dock. The hum was a low electric pulse, like a heartbeat under the floorboards. He'd lie awake and listen to it. In the morning it would go out again. It would go into the corners. It ate the dust and the lost things. Once, it found a Cheerio from a breakfast in March. It was there. Once, it nudged a slipper under the sofa. It did not find the slipper. It nudged it back. It didn't make sense.

Miriam had been dead for eleven months. The house still kept her shape. Her cardigan was still on the hook by the back door. Her glasses were on the table. They were waiting for a face. He hadn't vacuumed since the funeral. He'd swept the kitchen crumbs into the corners. The rest of the dust had gathered like a grey snow along the baseboards. The vacuum went after it. It had a bristled brush. It had a hunger for it. It was very small and very stubborn.

At first, he talked to it like he talked to the radio. It went for the tassels on Miriam's rug. He said, "Not there. You're going to get stuck." It got stuck. The tassels were wound around the brush. It stopped in the middle of the living room and said, "Error four, please clear my path." It was a woman's voice. It was a recorded voice. It was calm. Harold knelt. His knees cracked like ice on a puddle. He pulled the tassels free. He pulled them out one by one. It waited. It was patient. It was a stone. He said, "There. Go on."

Claire would call every Sunday. She would ask, "Is it working?" He said, "It's working." She would ask, "Are you letting it run?" He said, "I'm letting it run." Sometimes she would say, "Dad, are you eating?" He said, "I'm eating." He wasn't. The vacuum moved between them. It was a small, busy silence. She said, "You can name it in the app, Dad." He said, "I don't need an app to name something." She asked, "What did you name it?" He looked at the disc, docked, glowing. It had a little green eye in the dark. He said, "I didn't." But he had. He called it You. He used to call Miriam You. For forty years. You left the light on. You forgot the mail. You were there in the kitchen. It was humming.

It cleaned under the bed, which was a place he avoided. It came out with a hairpin, a nickel, and a dried petal from a rose. The rose he'd given her for no reason. It didn't bring them to him. It just went on. It dragged its shadow across the floor. Sometimes, at night, he heard it knock against the wall in the next room. For half a second, he thought someone else was awake.

One afternoon, it found the spot by the window. Miriam used to stand there to look at birds. The floor was worn pale. The vacuum went around it three times, as if reading Braille. Then it went on. Harold stood there. He had coffee. It was going cold. He wanted to say, she stood there. He wanted to say she said the cardinals were showing off. But there was no one to say it to. Except the machine. The machine only wanted the room clean.

It finished at dusk. The floor was shining. It was like a lake under the lamp. It went back to its dock. It clicked softly. Harold sat in his chair. The house was quiet. But it wasn't the same quiet. It was the quiet of a room that someone had been breathing in. The vacuum light blinked once, twice. It went dark. He leaned down. He touched the top of it. It was smooth. It was warm from its work. He said, "Good night." It didn't answer. Outside, the wind was moving through the bare branches. The floor was clean. It held the last of the light. He sat there. He was not alone. He was not quite.

text:
I grew up living in what I considered an urban environment. But when I moved to the other side of the country, I realized just how many trees they had. And I realized I hadn't appreciated the trees where I was growing up. I think it's the same as a lot of us. We don't appreciate the trees because they're everywhere, or they're not there. But in an urban environment, trees are infrastructure. They are so much more than decorative. I think we need to really make it a priority for our cities to have trees, to grow trees. They should not be an amenity. They should be infrastructure. So we need to start building our urban forests. And that's the conversation that I'm excited about. And I think it's a very urgent conversation.

And in terms of the environmental benefits, trees cool us. They provide shade. And if you're in a concrete city or an asphalt city, the urban heat island effect can really warm up the city. And it can be several degrees. And trees will help cool it down. And they do that in multiple ways. They provide shade, so they cool the surface. And they also cool the air. So it's a multi-faceted benefit. And it helps us to avoid heat-related illnesses and even deaths. And then trees help us with air quality. They filter particulate matter, they absorb carbon dioxide, they release oxygen, etc. And they help with water management. Their roots and leaves capture water, and that reduces flooding and eases the burden on our stormwater infrastructure. And we're seeing more extreme weather events, so we're seeing more extreme precipitation events. And so trees help us deal with that. So that's the environmental benefit, which is the most urgent.

But then beyond that, there are benefits to our mental health, to our physical health, to our sense of well-being. And there's a lot of research on that. And I think there's a lot of research showing that access to green space helps reduce stress, helps with concentration, helps with mental health. And for kids, it's great to have places to play and to explore. And for adults, it's nice to have a walk under a canopy. And it can lower blood pressure, it can restore attention, etc. And for hospitals, it's been shown that hospitals that have views of trees, patients recover faster, they need less pain medication, etc. And so it's really good for our health. And I think in a society where we're realizing the cost of loneliness, the cost of being sedentary, etc., it's really good to have that free, public, therapeutic benefit that trees provide.

And then there's community benefits. Trees help bring community. If a neighborhood has good trees, people spend more time outdoors. They look out for each other. They walk around. And so it can really help with crime. And there are economic benefits, too. If you have a neighborhood with good trees, property values go up. And if you have a good tree canopy, it makes the neighborhood more walkable, it makes people less reliant on cars, it helps with public transit, it helps with local businesses. And so it helps the local economy. And then there's an equity component, because the places that have the least trees, the places that are the most urbanized, the places that have the most pollution, the places that have the most heat, those are often the low-income neighborhoods. And so it's really important that we plant trees equitably and make sure that the places that need them the most are the places that we're planting them. And that's really, really important.

But the challenges are, planting trees is hard. It costs money. It takes a lot of water. It takes a lot of maintenance. If you plant a young tree and don't take care of it, it will die. And if you plant the wrong species, it can be a problem. It can crack sidewalks, it can block views, it can worsen allergies. And people worry that if we put trees in, it will increase rents and displace people. And that's a real phenomenon called green gentrification. And so we need to be mindful of that. And we need to be mindful of all these things. And we need to have community engagement, we need to have the right species, we need to have the right maintenance, we need to have the right planning. But it's not a reason to not do it. It's a reason to do it well. And the alternative of having a city with no trees is much worse. And so I think it's worth it. And I think we should be investing in trees as a priority. And I think it's really important to think about it as infrastructure, not as an amenity.

text:
The kennel just hummed with noise. Barking, little shrieks, the clatter of metal bowls hitting the floor. It all broke off the concrete walls and fell back down in pieces. Mara walked down the line, hands shoved deep in her pockets. Every single dog was looking at her. I don't know if you can truly ignore that weight. A beagle was running in tight circles. A shepherd kept ramming its face right up to the wire. The smell was awful, that strong pine cleaner scent trying to mask something older and sadder. It was wet fur. She came here to pick up a dog. But I don't know if I felt like she deserved one. Or if her life had enough room in it for another heartbeat.

Denise was walking in front of her. "Most of these guys are just scared," Denise said. "They don't know why they're here. They only know they were somewhere else, and then they weren't."

Mara just nodded. She had been somewhere else once, too. Then she wasn't. The house was so quiet. It didn't feel like peace. It felt like a held breath.

In the end of the row, in the last cage, there was a small brown dog. She lay curled up like a comma. She wasn't barking. She wasn't wagging her tail. She was barely there. A bundle of ribs and matted fur, one ear folded the wrong way. When Mara stopped, the dog lifted her head. Then she lowered it back down. It was like she'd learned not to open the door of hope.

"This is Juniper," Denise said. "We think she's about three. Came in as a stray. She's been here six weeks. She won't eat when people watch her. She shakes if you reach too fast."

Mara knelt down. The concrete was really rough, it bit into her knees. She didn't reach in. She just sat there, breathing, while all the other dogs made their racket. Juniper watched her from the back of the cage. Her eyes were the color of dark tea. Minutes passed.

"You don't have to pick today," Denise said gently.

"I know," Mara said. But she didn't move. She was thinking about how her mother used to say that animals choose you, not the other way around. She had really wanted that to be true.

Finally, Juniper crept forward. Low to the ground, like the floor might open. She stopped just an inch from the wire. Her nose twitched. Mara slid her fingers through the gap. The dog sniffed once, twice, then licked the tip of her finger. It was a quick, rough apology.

"Hey," Mara whispered. "Hey, little one."

Denise smiled but didn't say anything. Some things don't need to be said aloud.

The paperwork took an hour. They gave her a cardboard box of food. A faded rose leash. A folder of instructions. Juniper rode home in the passenger seat. She was trembling so hard the whole car seemed to hum. Mara drove slowly, taking corners like a boat through fog. At stoplights, she would rest her hand on the seat beside the dog. Not touching. Just near.

Her house smelled of lemon polish and old wood. She put a bed in the corner of the kitchen. A bowl of water. A chew toy shaped like a duck. Juniper went straight under the table and stayed there. Mara sat on the floor a few feet away. She read aloud from a magazine. Her voice was low and steady. She was reading about gardening. About nothing at all. The words filled the room like a lamp left on.

The first night, Juniper cried. It was a thin, high sound. More like wind than voice. Mara lay in bed with her eyes open, listening. She wanted to go to her, but she knew that sometimes comfort had to be offered without demand. In the morning, she found the dog still under the table, but the water bowl was empty.

Days passed. Juniper learned the sound of the refrigerator. The click of the leash. How Mara sighed when she came home. She still flinched at sudden movements. She still wouldn't eat if Mara stood too close. But she began to follow her from room to room. A quiet shadow with worried eyes.

A yoga studio can look very simple. You walk in and see mats, lights, sounds. But it is also a business, a community center, and a pretty tightly managed schedule. To see how it works, look at a student experience and then look behind the scenes. Every studio is different, but most have a common rhythm. People come in, teachers teach, staff manage membership and logistics, and it is all kept in a state where people can concentrate on breathing and movement.

First, there is the front desk. That is where you turn a visitor into a participant. Staff will greet you, check you in, get waivers, tell you where shoes and bags and coats go. New people get an orientation, where props are, how to set up a mat, what to expect. The front desk is also where you pay, where you get packages, where you buy memberships, where you book. It is the social heart of the studio, the place where questions get answered, where regulars start to see each other and talk.

Then, the schedule. That determines how the studio runs. There are different styles. Hatha, vinyasa, yin, restorative, power, hot. They are usually labeled by level, so you can choose the right thing. You have early morning classes, midday classes, evening classes, weekend workshops, teacher training. It is a balancing act. They balance popularity and profitability. If a class is always full, they add it. If a class is always empty, they change it or get rid of it. They balance it with room size, teacher availability, what is seasonal.

Teachers are the core of it. A yoga teacher is not just leading poses. A teacher reads the room. It is safe sequencing, offering modifications, demonstrating options, creating an environment where people can concentrate. A good teacher is watching for strain, adjusting language to different levels, knowing when to push and when to back off. They come early, they set up the music, set up the lighting, they stay after, they answer questions. Teachers are usually contractors, paid per class, paid by headcount, or flat rate. Most teachers teach at multiple studios to make their schedule.

The business model. Revenue is drop-in, class passes, memberships, workshops, retail, teacher training. Expenses are rent, utilities, insurance, cleaning, props, booking software, marketing, teacher pay. Rent is fixed. If a class is empty, rent is still coming. So they are dependent on memberships, on regulars, to be consistent. They have intro deals to get you in, then try to convert you to a member. Some are for profit, some are nonprofits, coops, community spaces, sliding scale.

Physical space. It takes constant care. The floor has to be clean, safe. Temperature, humidity. Props get replaced, organized. Sound, lighting, mirrors, ventilation. Behind the scenes, staff manage bookings, waitlists, cancellations, refunds, communication. Marketing, social media, email newsletters, community events. Hot yoga places need really good heating and ventilation. Restorative places need quiet and soft lights.

Finally, the community. Regulars become friends. Teachers learn your name, learn your injury, learn your story. It can become a refuge, a place to go. They host retreats, workshops, charity classes, meditation. That is part of retention. People go back because it is a place they belong, not just a workout. But they have to be mindful of boundaries. It should feel welcoming, not cliquish. Teachers have to be ethical, safe.

So, it is people, practice, and management. You come in, you check in, you get scheduled in a class. Teachers teach safely, with variation. The business makes money, controls costs. The space is comfortable and safe. It is not just a room with bodies on mats. When it works, it is a place where you practice physical health, mental calm, and connection.

I really did not anticipate finding philosophy on a used car lot. Not somewhere stuck between an inflatable tube man and a row of sedans with mismatched hubcaps. Yet that is where I went. Used car lots have this way of making you think about time. Last Saturday, I was standing on a lot that shimmered in the heat. It was a wide sea of asphalt, dotted with vehicles. Every single one of those cars had been loved, or neglected, or simply outgrown by someone else. There was a red compact right next to a silver minivan, and a pickup truck looming over both like an older brother who had seen things. Each one had a paper sticker in the windshield. A price written in bold marker, as if a number could summarize a whole history.

I was there because my own car had started to feel like a friend who kept canceling plans. The check engine light was a permanent passenger now. It just sat there, glowing with quiet judgment. It still started, mostly. But it rattled over bumps. It hesitated at intersections. It felt like it was thinking too hard about every decision. I needed something dependable. I did not want to pay for new. That is how I ended up walking past lines of cars whose odometers read like opening lines of novels.

A salesman named Daryl came out of the glass booth. He had a clipboard. His handshake was firm without being punishing. His smile was wide and practiced, not unkind. He asked what I was looking for. I said reliability. He nodded. Like I had named a rare and admirable virtue. Then he led me through the lot, talking about previous owners. It was like a librarian talking about characters in books. A schoolteacher who drove only to church. A retiree who kept every receipt. A teenager who probably treated the gas pedal like a video game controller.

The car I noticed first was a compact with a silver exterior. The interior smelled of lemon air freshener and faint coffee. The engine turned over with a sound like someone clearing their throat before speaking. The odometer showed eighty-nine thousand miles. That felt both frightening and strangely comforting. A car with that many miles had a past. It had been somewhere. It had carried people through weather, arguments, errands. Maybe a few good songs.

Daryl handed me the keys. We took it onto the highway. The road unspooled beneath us, gray and ordinary. The tires hummed. The steering pulled just slightly to the right, a detail I pretended not to notice. Daryl talked about warranty options and financing. Numbers floating through the air like weather. I asked if it had been in an accident. He paused for a breath. Then said no. I did not know whether to believe him. Trust, I realized, is its own kind of test drive.

Back at the dealership, we sat in the glass booth and negotiated. The air conditioner hummed. Through the window, I could see my old car parked near the trade-in lane. It looked smaller and sadder than I remembered. It had carried me through moves, heartbreaks, road trips, and grocery runs. It was not just a machine. It was a scrapbook with wheels. I felt a pang of betrayal, then a pang of relief.

We agreed on a price. We signed papers. I took the new key, which felt heavier than it should have. As I drove off the lot, the tube man kept waving behind me. Selling something to the empty air. I thought about how we are all used cars in a way. We arrive with mileage, scratches, and stories we do not fully disclose. We hope someone will look past the dents and see what still runs true. The car I bought was not perfect. It had a small rattle. There was a stain on the backseat shaped like a tiny country. But it started every morning. And maybe that is enough. Not new, not flawless, but willing to go. I drove home with the windows down. Letting the ordinary road feel like an open page.

For days afterward, I kept thinking about the lot. The heat, the stickers, the quiet arithmetic of hope. A used car is a compromise, but compromise is not always defeat. Sometimes it is simply the shape of moving forward when perfection is not for sale. The key in my pocket was a small promise. Scratched but serviceable. And that felt honest.

I never liked it. The uniform. It smelled of industrial detergent, the kind that has a chemical ring to it, and underneath all that harsh chemical, there was this sweet, faint ghost of cedar. The cedar was all in the closet. It wasn't in the clothes. The uniform itself was a stiff navy blue polyester blend. Polyester has this irritatingness to it. It doesn't drape. It just stands away from your body. It's like a suit of armor. And it doesn't let the light through. When Ms. Albright, that was her teacher, she would hold it up to the window, you'd see the shadow on the floor. She remembered that. It was like a rectangle of nothing. It was opaque. And she hated it. And the collar was starched. The collar was this pointy V that would rub against your neck. She hated it. It would irritate her. It would be a constant, low-grade irritation, like a pebble in your shoe.

And now, thirty years later, she's in her classroom. And the kids are wearing uniforms. And she watches them and thinks, it's the same. The uniform is a great equalizer. It erases things. And she hates that. It erases who they are. They're all the same. It's all navy and white. And it's softer. It's cotton now. It's a little more forgiving. But it's still the same.

And there's a boy, Leo, in the back. And he's new. And his uniform is too big. And he's pulling at the collar, picking at the button. And he's got a paperclip thing on his desk. And it's a cathedral. It's a spaceship. It's something. It's a rebellion. And she walks over, and she kneels down. And she says, it's beautiful. What is it? And he says, it's just a thing. And she says, it looks like a place you'd want to live. A place with no rules. And he smiles. Just a little. And then he looks at her and sees that she's got a grey suit and sensible shoes. And he looks away. And she thinks, he sees the uniform. He sees the authority. He's in a uniform, and she's in a uniform. And he's been erased.

And then she watches him during recess. And he's by the fence. And he's apart from the kickball game. And the kids are just a galaxy, just swirling and shouting. And he's this tiny planet on the edge. And he's just tracing patterns in the dust. And she thinks, the uniform is supposed to make him part of the group. And it makes him more isolated. It's a costume. It's a play he doesn't understand.

And then she gets a note. And it's from a girl, Chloe. And she's very shy. And the note says, Leo's paperclip thing was cool. And she looks at Chloe. And Chloe's uniform is perfect. And she's a model student. And she's got it right. And she sees the thing. And she sees him. And it's beautiful.

And then the bell rings. And the kids go. And she's just there. And she thinks about her uniform. And she thinks about how she felt erased. And she thinks about how she spent her career trying to see the child under the cloth. To see the person that the uniform was supposed to hide. And then she sees the thing. And the thing is still there. And there's a button. And the button is from his uniform. And it's just a button. And she picks it up. And it's smooth. And it's cool. And it's nothing. And she puts it in her hand. And it's a gift. And it's a quiet acknowledgement. And she closes her hand. And it's a weight. And it's a circle. And it's perfect.

I have been travelling across the Alps on trains a number of times and I have to say this is one of the most spectacular things you can do. But if you are going to do it, I think you need to really understand how it works. Why? Because the railway is a feat of engineering and the engineering is incredible. And the great thing is that when you're on a train, it is so smooth, it is so easy, and the views are so spectacular that you forget how hard it is. I mean, it is a mountain crossing. It's the sort of thing that for centuries was just impossible. And then in the 1800s, the engineers came along and said, well, we can actually do this. And they did it, and they did it beautifully.

So, how do they do it? Well, first of all, the journey starts in a city, probably. For example, the Bernina line goes from Chur in Switzerland down to Tirano in Italy. The farmers market started like the tide. First it was nothing, then it crept up and then it just arrived and it was full. By seven the square was completely filled with the white tents and they were snapping in the wind, and their shadows were stretched out long and blue across the bricks. I came early, I always come early, with my folding table under one arm and a crate of tomatoes under the other. The tomatoes are not perfect. Some of them are split at the shoulder. Some have black freckles on them. But they smell of sun and dust. And I put them out in a nice pyramid, like jewels.

Across the aisle there's a woman called June, she does honey, and it's in jars that are the colour of late afternoon, and she waves at me. I'm wearing gloves, so I wave back. She says, you're late, the early birds bought the basil. And I say, let them, I'm here for the quiet. But the quiet never really lasts. The market starts to fill with noise. There's a guitar being played and there's a coffee urn hissing, and there's the clack of a knife on a chopping board. There's a little girl in yellow boots who has her nose pressed up to the glass where June's honey display is. There's a man in a linen apron who's arguing gently with a customer over the price of chard. And the air smells of wet earth, cinnamon, frying onion, and the sweet animal breath of peaches. And I stand behind my tomatoes and I look over my little red kingdom, and I feel like the keeper of this small world.

I've been coming to this market for thirty years. At first I came with my wife, Lena. She'd always buy flowers, even when we didn't have money for bread. Now I come alone. But my mind is a strange thing. It still expects to see her at the corner, with her head tilted to one side like a bird, listening to the rain, or listening to the stems of the sunflowers. It keeps the furniture in the same place, even when no one has been in there for a long time.

A boy comes up to my table. He's about nine. He's got a cowlick in his hair. Very serious. He's holding a five-dollar bill in his fist, like a flag. He says, are these yours? I say, yes. And he says, they're ugly. And I laugh. I say, they are. But they taste like the ones your grandmother used to grow. And he thinks about this. And he says, my grandmother doesn't grow tomatoes, she grows roses. And I say, well, then she'd know, roses and tomatoes both need patience. And he buys two tomatoes and carries them off, like they're eggs. I watch him go until he disappears into the crowd. And then the wind changes, and I smell rain from the west. And everyone starts looking at the sky. June covers her honey jars with a cloth. The guitar player sings a song about a river that runs on, even when nobody's watching.

By noon the market is thinning. I've sold almost everything. I'm packing my empty crate, folding my table. And I stand there for a moment. And I watch the tents flapping, like tired wings. And I see a woman buy the last of June's honey. And June smiles. And it's not a smile for the sale. It's a smile for the day, for making it through. And I walk past the flower stall. And there's a bucket of sunflowers on the edge of the pavement. And they're all turned towards the vanishing sun. And I stop. I haven't bought flowers in years. I felt it was a betrayal or a waste, or both. But there's the girl in the yellow boots again. She's holding a stem. And her mother is laughing at something the florist says. And it's bright and ordinary. And I remember Lena saying, markets are just kitchens with no walls. Everyone trading hunger and hope in the same open air. I didn't believe it then. I do now.

So I reach in my pocket. I buy a sunflower. I don't know why. And I walk home. The streets smell of rain. And the flower nods against my shoulder, like a small forgiving head. And the market, and Lena, and all the quiet Saturdays, settle around me, like a gentle, unasked-for grace.

I've never cancelled my gym membership. I've been at the same gym for about 10 years now, and I have made a pact with myself that if I go 3 weeks or more without going, I will cancel. I've done it twice. And it's just that. Cancel. No guilt. It is a business transaction. It's not like a relationship.
But I know everyone who has a gym membership. They should not have it. They should either go or cancel. So many people keep paying for the gym they go to once a month, or even once every two months. And we're paying like 50, 60, 70 dollars a month. And it's just ridiculous. I mean, we're paying like 500, 600 dollars a year, and we're going once a month. And for some people it's even worse. They don't even go.
I think it's a bit of a psychological thing. You feel like, if I go to the gym, it means I'm disciplined. If I don't, it means I'm not. So it's like, I have to keep paying, otherwise I'm not disciplined. And it's really, really not. You can be disciplined at home. You can walk. You can run. You can do stuff. You don't need a gym. But then it's very easy to say, I don't have a gym, I can't go to the gym. And that's just a story we tell ourselves.
The other thing that I think is interesting, the other psychological thing, is that people think that if they keep paying, then they will go. That's not true. Paying doesn't make you go. Going makes you go. So if you're paying and not going, you're just wasting money.
The reality is, I know people who are really committed to the gym. And it's not even about the gym. They just like to be in a space where there are other people working out. They like the atmosphere. They like the structure of it. For them, it's worth it. They go 3, 4 times a week. And it's fantastic.
But then, for other people, they just don't. And I think that's really common. It's common for people to sign up for a gym membership at the start of the year, or at the start of the month, or just after the holidays, and then they will go for two weeks, maybe three weeks, and then they stop. And they keep paying. And it's just sad.
But I think the best thing to do, if you're not going, is to cancel. I really think so. If you're not going, cancel. And then, if you want to go, sign up again. It's not a big deal.

text:
The pitch for remote work has always been about freedom. You skip the commute, skip the cubicle, and get to set your own hours. But for a lot of people, all that flexibility just pushes you off the map of the office and the daily human contact that used to happen. This is one of the interesting things about loneliness. It is not the same thing as being alone. Plenty of people sit alone in a crowded room and don't mind. The problem is the gap between the amount of connection a person is looking for and what they are actually getting.
I don't think working from home makes you lonely, not automatically. But it takes all the accidental social stuff that would happen in an office and removes it. Now if you want to talk to someone you actually have to make a point of it. And that's a pretty big deal.
Humans are profoundly social animals. Chronic loneliness is associated with depression, anxiety, heart problems, bad sleep, cognitive decline, etc. There are a number of reasons why working from home might feed loneliness.
The first is all of this stuff that we are losing. When you go into an office, some of it is a social exercise. You're going to a meeting, you're going to grab a coffee, you're overhearing a joke in the kitchen, asking someone a question. This is all ambient sociality. When you're working from home, that sociality goes away. Everything becomes an intentional event. You have a call, you have a message, you have a calendar invite. When all your socializing is intentional, you can go days without being touched by the warmth of a colleague. And so the isolation creeps in.
The second is that communication is narrower. When I'm on a video call, it's just the words and the face. We lose a lot of the peripheral things, the shared context of the environment. Sometimes it feels very transactional. A lot of people will report Zoom fatigue, this sense that meetings are about status and tasks, not about relationship. If we're just doing chat, it's efficient, but it's not as rich, it's not as easy to read the tone. And so you get lots of shallow contact, but it doesn't feel like deep contact. And it can even be more tiring.
The third is this blurring of boundaries. When I have a job, I used to have a commute. And now that I don't have a commute, I might be working earlier, I might be working later, I might be answering messages at night. And so my home becomes my office, and my office never closes. And I'm too depleted to do other things. I'm not doing a lot of socializing. And at the same time, I've lost this social support that was in the office. So I have less social support, and more work related stress.
Fourth, I think it's unequal. It's not uniform. Some people will love it. They have a partner, they have friends, they have established networks. They're experienced. They're extroverted. But early career people, or people who have just moved into a new city, or people who don't have a network, or people who are immigrants, or people who are neurodivergent, or people who are introverts, or people who live alone, these are the people who really struggle. So, for instance, if I'm a new hire, I don't get the benefits of socializing at the office, or getting onboarding, or the informal learning that happens when you're just hanging around a company. Or if I live alone, I might go whole days without face to face contact. Or if I have caregiving responsibilities, I'm surrounded by family, but I don't have adult peers. So this is very unequal. But for some people, working from home is a lifeline. For disabled people, for introverts, for people who experience discrimination in the office, it's really important.
So it's not all bad. But it's really important to have a design mindset. So I think that companies can do a lot to reduce loneliness. Things like virtual coffees, but without a clear agenda, mentorship programs, employee resource groups, regular 1:1s that are not just about work. And also, some sort of in person touchpoint, even if it's once a quarter. And I think that managers can be really helpful. They can model boundaries, not sending messages at night, not expecting to be available at all times.
And individuals can do things. For example, schedule social contact. Treat it like a meeting. Join a coworking space, join a club, take a class. Have a ritual. Maybe I walk with my neighbor once a week, or I call a friend at lunch, or I have a game night. And set boundaries. Have an end of day, and have a physical separation. And sometimes, therapy, and support groups are very important. Especially if this becomes chronic, if you have anxiety or depression. And recognize that this is a signal, not a verdict. That it's an indication of a need, and that you can work on it.
So to summarize, I think that remote work and loneliness are linked, because remote work takes away all the accidental, embodied, boundary-setting stuff that office work provides. And so, communication is more intentional, it's narrower, it's easier to delay. And it's highest risk for people who don't have outside networks, or early career people. But I think it's not a given. And I think that if we're intentional about it, and we create boundaries, and we create rituals, and we have mentorship and in person touchpoints, we can have flexibility and we can have belonging. And I think that's really important to get right.

text:
I dont really like audio guides, but I have done some research on them and the reality is they can be really great. They are not just convenience things that are good for people who dont want to read things. They can actually be used really well. But for me, I have been through museums where I put the headphones on, walked through the gallery and I was looking at my phone or the number on the wall, not the object. So, the audio guide can be an interpretive tool, but it should be optional, it should be well designed, and you should use it sparingly. But if it takes over your own looking, your own thinking, your own feeling, it becomes a problem.

The biggest argument for audio guides, and its a very powerful argument, is access. Museums have objects that you cannot necessarily understand on their own. So a guide can help to explain the iconography, the history, the materials, the provenance, the controversies. It can help to translate very specialist language into interesting narrative. So that is really good. And it is really good for people who are blind or have low vision, to have audio description. It is really good for people who are not native speakers, to have audio guides in multiple languages. It is really good for children, for casual visitors, to have a guide that helps them to make sense of a room of objects. It gives them a story, it gives them characters, it gives them conflict, it gives them discovery. And it lets people move at their own pace. So, you can pause, you can replay, you can skip. So, in that sense, it is a really great tool. It is a tool for democratizing the museum. It is a tool for giving people access to expert interpretation without having to pay for a human guide, or having knowledge yourself.

But, it can be a problem as well. And the problem is, the same way that it can be a mediator, it can be a weakening of the experience. Because the guide tells you what to look at, it tells you what to feel. So, you might be looking at a painting and it might be really puzzling or really moving, and then the guide gives you the answer. And you might say, oh, that is really interesting. And then you move on to the next one. And you get this kind of check-box tourism, you see this object, you hear the number, you move on. And the other problem is, headphones isolate you. So, you are not having a conversation with your companions, you are not having those spontaneous moments where you are walking through the museum and you see something together and you react to it together. And that is what makes museums really memorable. And if the guide is too long, it is too detailed, then you get cognitive overload. So, you are spending more energy following the guide than looking at the object. And if there are technical problems, if the interface is bad, if it is crowded, the guide can become a problem. And the other thing is, not everything needs a story. And silence, ambiguity, and just looking and thinking, are part of the museum experience.

So, its not an inherently bad thing, but its a question of design and its a question of how you use it. And I think that a good guide should be brief, it should be optional, it should be layered, it should be something that helps you to orient yourself, not a lecture. And it should be something that asks questions, not something that gives answers. And it should be something that directs your attention to the object. So, not, this painting is about despair, but, look at the brushwork here, look at what is happening at the left hand side of this painting. And museums can do this well. Museums can have multiple voices, they can have the curator, they can have the artist, they can have community members, they can have critics, so that there is no single voice. And then you can use the guide as a scaffold. So, you listen for a few minutes, then you take the headphones off, and you go up close and you look at the object and let it speak for itself.

So, its not a bad thing, its not a substitute for art, its not a betrayal of authenticity, its a tool. And like any tool, it can help you or it can distort you. And I think the greatest value of audio guides is that they open doors. They give you context, they give you access, they help people who are intimidated by objects that they are not familiar with. And the greatest risk is that they become a closed corridor, a predetermined path, and you are not allowed to be curious. So, I think the ideal is a rhythm of listening and looking, guidance and freedom. And if the audio guide helps you see more deeply, its doing its job. If it stops you seeing, turn it off.

text:
I was confused why I came, and I was still confused when I was standing at the gate. Three months now since my grandma left. The garden is feral. Morning glories are all over the rusted trellis, climbing it, they look like little blue hands. Her roses have thrown out canes all over, thorny and unrepentant. Knee-high grass around the birdbath. There was a robin in there, bathing, as if nothing has changed. I had my keys and a paper bag of groceries. House is empty, sold to young couple. They wanted to renovate. They gave me till Sunday to take what I want. What I want isn't in the house. It's out here. In the damp earth and the smell of tomato leaves. In the crooked row of lavender she insisted grew better when you ignored it.

She taught me to garden the summer I turned nine. After my parents divorced. She said you don't yank the roots, you ask the soil for what you need, gently. She was kneeling next to me, hands spotted and sure. Straw hat with the torn brim, man's denim shirt. Smelled like sunscreen and mint. I remember thinking she was the oldest thing in the world, and the kindest.

She lives in a memory care unit now, forty minutes away. Hall smells like disinfectant and lemon cake. She doesn't recognize me much. Last week I went and she looked past me, out the window, and said the tomatoes need staking. I said they do. She said use the twine in the shed. Not the green one, the brown. I said I will. She nodded, satisfied, closed her eyes. And she was gone for a moment again.

I put the groceries on the porch, walked into the garden. Gate creaks like an old man. Inside it's thick, green, humid cathedral of leaves. Peony bushes collapsed under their own blooms, petals browning at the edges. The stone path she laid herself, one flat rock at a time, is barely visible under creeping thyme. I knelt, pulled a handful of weeds. Soil cool, loose, alive with worms.

Voice behind me. You're going to get your hands dirty. I turned. Mrs. Alvarez, the neighbor, stood at the fence with a trowel. She's been there forty years. Shared tomatoes and gossip with grandma, once a bottle of whiskey on New Year's Eve. I said I don't mind. She said she'd be glad someone was tending it. She used to say a garden is a conversation, if you stop talking it forgets you. I laughed, but it came out like a cough. She's forgetting a lot these days. Her face softened. Not this. Not the garden. She asks about it every time I visit. Wants to know if the figs are ripe. I said they aren't, not yet. She said then you'll have to tell her when they are.

She went back to her yard, I was alone. Worked without gloves, pulled weeds till my nails were black. Found the twine in the shed, brown and frayed, tied the tomatoes to their stakes. Leaves smell sharp and green, like my grandma's hands. I talked to the plants, softly, the way she did. There. There you go.

By late afternoon sun had shifted, garden looked less wild. Not restored, that takes seasons, but acknowledged. Roses still sprawled, but I cut back the worst of the canes. Lavender stood in its crooked row, forgiving. I sat on the stone bench by the birdbath, watched a bee stumble into a foxglove. Light was gold and slanted, the way it is before evening, everything seems briefly possible.

Phone buzzed. Memory care. I answered. Hello. Miss, a nurse's voice, gentle. Your grandmother is asking for you. Says she wants to tell you something about the garden. Throat tightened. I said I'll be there in forty. Drove with the windows down, cut grass and exhaust. Arrived, she was in a chair by the window, blanket over her knees. She looked smaller than I remembered, like a bird in winter.

She said you came. I said I did. She reached for my hand, her fingers were cold, but her grip was surprisingly strong. She said the tomatoes. I said I staked them, with the brown twine. She smiled, slow, distant. Good girl. And the figs? I said not yet. She said they'll come, you have to wait. I nodded. We sat in silence, watching light fade through blinds. Parking lot outside was gray and ordinary, but in my mind I saw the garden, green and breathing, tomatoes leaning toward the sun. I squeezed her hand, she squeezed back. For a moment we were both in the same place. Then her eyes drifted closed, and I stayed, holding on, until the nurse came to say it was time to go.

Drove home in the dark. When I got to the house, I stood at the gate, listened. Crickets loud. Garden quiet. But it was still there, waiting.

Last Saturday, I was dusting the bookshelf in the hallway. I pulled down a hardcover. My grandmother had given it to me years ago. The dust jacket is long gone. The spine had turned the color of weak tea. It was soft, too. I opened it, and something fell out. It was a photograph. It was small and square. It had scalloped edges. They looked like a row of tiny waves. I picked it up and turned it over. There was no date on it. No name. Just a faded chemical smell. And a thumbprint. It was faint. It was in the corner.

The image was black and white. But it must have been a bright day. A young woman was standing under a tree. She was tipping her head back, laughing. She had one hand pressing a hat to her hair. Next to her was a young man. His shirt had rolled sleeves. He was looking at her. Not the camera. It was like she was the only weather that mattered. It took me a long moment to recognize my grandmother. All I knew was her as old. Soft arms. Hard candies. Her voice crackled. It was like a radio tuned to a faraway station. But here she was. Maybe nineteen. She was radiant. Unguarded. A stranger. But I was related to her.

I sat on the floor. The book was still open on my knees. I had read this novel in college. The margins were full of my own younger certainties. How strange it was. This photograph had been living in there all along. Pressed against a story about longing and time. I had moved this book from apartment to apartment. Never looked inside. It didn't feel like an accident. More like a message. Something I wasn't ready to receive. I realized that books aren't just containers for words. They are shelves. For the selves we forget to remember.

I looked at the photograph a while. The details started to speak. The tree was an elm. Its branches were a green cathedral in the background. The hat was straw. The dress was light. Sleeveless. The young man's smile was crooked. It was sincere. I wondered who took the picture. What happened after the shutter clicked. Did they walk to a lake? Did they argue? Did they marry? Did they know how quickly the afternoon would become an artifact? My grandmother never told me about that day. Maybe she forgot. Maybe she just chose not to carry it forward. Memory is a river. We are all trying to cup it in our hands.

I didn't put the photograph back. I set it on my desk. It sits there now. Leaning against a jar of pens. Sometimes I catch it from the corner of my eye. I feel a tug. Something I cannot name. It is not exactly grief. Though it is close. It is the ache of understanding. Every old person I have loved was once a young person. One I will never meet. Every ordinary afternoon. Like this one. Is already becoming a photograph. For someone else to find. The book remains on the shelf. A little lighter now. But I like to think the photograph is finally where it belongs. Not hidden between pages. Out in the light. Reminding me that the past is never truly past. It is only waiting. Quietly. For us to open the right book and look.

It was a promise. When I first unlocked the door to my apartment after closing, I was expecting a hit of triumph. I did not get it. What I got was a small vertigo. I was standing inside a promise. The rooms are smaller than I remember. The ceiling is lower, the windows dirty. The kitchen cabinets are a little crooked and they look exhausted. The bathroom has tiles that have a yellowed grin. So, you start. Renovation starts as fantasy. You are looking at pictures of nice spaces, airy and bright, and you imagine your life in it. You imagine your life moving into the space. And then the contractor comes. There is a crowbar. Fantasy meets dust. The first day of demolition was the loudest day of my life. It was horrible. Walls opened up. They opened up like mouths. The work was not romantic. It was very messy. The estimates were always swelled like bread. Estimates always swelled like bread. And I had to make decisions that felt absurdly consequential. Which white? Which gray? Which tile will I still love in ten years? I stood in a home improvement store, holding samples under fluorescent light, trying to predict my future self. Do you want light or storage? Do you want a place for guests or a place for solitude? And every choice is a small confession.

I chose a pale oak floor. Because I liked it. It reminded me of a beach I visited as a child. It reminded me of a beach. Warm boards under bare feet. And I chose a deep green for the kitchen cabinets. Because it felt like a forest after rain. It felt like a forest after rain. And I chose a simple white tile for the bathroom. Because I wanted it to feel clean. I wanted it to feel uncomplicated. None of these choices were grand. They were just mine. In the middle of all this dust, that mattered. That it was mine.

And then it happened. The transformation happened slowly and then all at once. One afternoon, the floor was finished. And it just seemed to exhale. It was the same address, the same square footage. But it was no longer the place I bought. It was the place I made. The light traveled farther. The light traveled farther than it used to. The room seemed to expand. The new cabinets stood straight. And then, for a long time after the work ended, I kept noticing the absence of noise. The hammering had become a kind of company. And its disappearance left a ringing silence. But it taught me that making is never finished. Making is never finished. A home is not a museum piece. A home is not a photograph. Within a week, the first scratch appeared on the floor.
